headline: Telangana HC: Joint Commissioner competent for Section 122 CGST penalty above ₹2 crore; writ dismissed
reference: M/s Charanji Distributors v. Principal Commissioner of Central Tax & Ors., W.P. No. 14136 of 2026, Telangana High Court, 13.10.2026
summary_points: Issue: whether SCN (17.02.2025) and Order-in-Original (15.10.2025) under Section 122 CGST were void as no proper officer was assigned before Circular 254/11/2025-GST.
Held: Circular dated 27.10.2025 makes the Joint Commissioner proper officer for cases above ₹2 crore; the OIO was passed by a Joint Commissioner.
Court relied on Section 160 CGST to hold the order cannot be challenged merely on this ground; the jurisdiction plea was rejected and the writ dismissed.
Other pleas (double penalty, natural justice, service, statements) were left to the appellate authority, as the OIO is appealable; merits not examined.
Time spent on the writ may be excluded for limitation in appeal, subject to Section 14 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
who_is_affected: Taxpayers facing Section 122 penalty proceedings (including ₹17.27 crore ITC-related penalty), and GST professionals challenging adjudication on proper-officer jurisdiction.
action_required: File an appeal before the appellate authority to raise merits and natural justice pleas within limitation, rather than relying on a jurisdictional writ challenge.

Telangana High Court has dismissed a writ petition by M/s Charanji Distributors challenging a Section 122 CGST penalty order, which proposed a penalty linked to ITC of ₹17.27 crore.

The petitioner argued that no proper officer had been assigned for Section 122 before CBIC Circular 254/11/2025-GST dated 27.10.2025, so the show-cause notice and order were void.

The Court noted that the circular came after both the notice and the order. However, it designates the Joint Commissioner as the proper officer for cases above ₹2 crore, and the order was passed by a Joint Commissioner. Relying on Section 160 CGST, it held the order cannot be assailed merely on this ground.

Other contentions, including double penalisation, service of notice and reliance on statements, were left open for the appellate authority since the order is appealable. The Court also allowed exclusion of time spent on the writ for limitation, subject to Section 14 of the Limitation Act.
